Nellie Bly wrote Ten Days in a Mad-House, her experience on Blackwell's Island, entered for copyright in 1887. Bly feigned insanity to reveal asylum horrors for the New York World. The book form followed a flood of letters, she says.

On the twenty-second of September the World asked whether she could get herself committed to an asylum and write a plain account of the treatment there. Bly agreed to pass the doctors and live a week among the insane without being found out. Her introduction reports a result: New York City appropriated a million dollars more each year for the care of the insane.

Comedian Dave Smith talks hyper-inflation and fractional reserve banking with Rogan in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Smith, a libertarian comic and podcaster, is the show's regular voice on money and the state. His act is half joke, half lecture, and this segment leans lecture.

He explains how banks create money by lending, and why he thinks the system quietly taxes savers through rising prices. Rogan asks what a normal person should do with savings in such a world. The segment is a plain-language brief for the hard-money view, from a comic who treats economics as a contact sport.
